transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess I’m here because I can’t get my mind to stop jumping around. Like, one minute I’m thinking our lab’s new partnership is going to mean they cut my position, and then I’m sure my data are wrong, and then I’m thinking about bills piling up.

And then it turns into, like, my family probably thinks I’m falling behind, or that I’ve already messed up my chances at grad school. I know that’s a lot of different things, sorry—I work in a lab, so it’s easy to start with one thing and then suddenly I’m thinking about everything that could go wrong.
Do these worries and anxious thoughts happen most days, and do they tend to jump between different areas of your life, even when there isn’t a specific stressor or event that’s triggering them?

Yeah, most days, I think. It’s not even like one clear thing happens and then I worry about that. It’s more like my brain just… starts scanning.

Like I’ll be at the lab and suddenly I’m thinking the new partnership means they’re going to cut my position, and then I’ll be worried my data are wrong, and then somehow I’m thinking about bills, and whether my family thinks I’m falling behind, and grad school—like I’ve already ruined my chances. It jumps around a lot.
Do you notice any physical sensations when these thoughts come up, like restlessness, feeling tense, or maybe trouble sleeping?

Yeah, definitely. At work especially I feel kind of wound up, like I can’t just sit in my chair and do the thing in front of me. I’ll be tapping my foot, checking messages even when I know nothing important came in, and then I’ll get up and walk back to the instrument room for no real reason.

And the normal lab sounds—like a door closing or something beeping—can make me jump, which is embarrassing because it’s a lab, noises happen all the time. I just feel… keyed up, I guess.
